title: Soft lease handoff and hot-standby orchestration for dedicated pools
body:
Summary:

This PRD proposes a "soft lease handoff" pattern plus a small hot-standby orchestration layer for Redwood Dedicated pools. The goal is to provide predictable, low-latency tenant switchover and short-duration burst capacity without sacrificing tenant isolation guarantees or KV/prefix cache value. The feature targets scenarios where tenants briefly exceed committed throughput, operators need fast recovery from preemption, and customers expect graceful service continuity during lease migration or pool maintenance.

Why this is different from existing approaches:
- Unlike simple burst-credit or prewarm pools, this design focuses on preserving per-tenant runtime state (KV cache, warmed kernels) across a controlled short handoff window, so QoE degradation is minimized during swaps.
- Instead of hard preemption and full reinitialization, the system coordinates a soft handshake between donor and recipient nodes to transfer ephemeral runtime state and traffic routing gradually.

Problem statement / motivation:
- Tenants on Dedicated occasionally need momentary extra throughput (microbursts, traffic spikes) or must be relocated (maintenance, noisy neighbor mitigation). Current options either: (a) cold failover + model reload (high latency and cost), or (b) permissive overcommit + noisy neighbor risk. We need a middle path that preserves low tail latency and model cache continuity while maintaining isolation and SLOs.

Goals:
- Provide a soft handoff protocol to move active tenant sessions between nodes with minimal latency spike (target: 95th percentile added latency < 200ms for short text generation requests, < 50ms for embedding calls).
- Support short-duration bursts by temporarily borrowing hot-standby capacity while guaranteeing no cross-tenant KV contamination and honoring tenant-level quotas/SLOs.
- Make the mechanism observable and auditable (traceable handoff events, cost attribution, and rollback hooks).
- Integrate with existing autoscaler and quota systems; minimal changes to the serving runtime API.

Non-goals:
- This is not a replacement for long-term migration (e.g. model version pinning across regions) or multi-hour capacity redistribution.
- Not intended to move persistent model weights between entirely different hardware types.

Concept and user flow (high level):
1) Trigger: handoff can be operator-initiated (maintenance), autoscaler-driven (node decommission), or demand-driven (tenant surpasses burst threshold and needs short-term extra resources).
2) Candidate selection: scheduler finds a hot-standby node in the same pool (or designated burst pool). Hot-standby nodes are prewarmed with compatible kernels and model variants, holding an ephemeral "standby lease" for one or more tenants.
3) Soft handshake: donor node begins cooperative slowdown of new request acceptance while streaming minimal ephemeral state metadata (KV cache diffs, prefix signatures, recent attention/seq hints) to standby.
4) Traffic shifting: traffic is gradually routed to the standby node via smart-router (canary style with percentage ramp). The serving runtime keeps a short-lived dual-write mode for state updates (both nodes apply updates for a configured grace window).
5) Finalization: after the grace window and a verification pass (latency checks, token loss checks), the original lease is released. Billing and SLO attributions are reconciled (burst charge applied to tenant or absorbed by pool).

Design details:
- Lease epochs and grace windows:
  - Every tenant lease has an epoch id. A soft handoff creates a new epoch after a configurable grace window (default 30s). During the window, donor and recipient accept new requests, with recipient operating at limited concurrency until warmed.
  - Grace window is adjustable per-tenant SLA: burst-friendly tenants get longer windows; strict isolation tenants get shorter ones.

- Standby prewarm policy:
  - Two standby modes: passive and active. Passive: kernels loaded, model weights resident but no KV state. Active: warmed with tenant-specific KV signature (privacy-preserving) and partial cache sync from recent traffic.
  - Standby assignment is affinity-based; prefer nodes in same failure domain/az to preserve latency.

- KV cache transfer & privacy:
  - We do NOT transfer raw KV logs. Instead we transfer compacted, integrity-checked diffs and prefix signatures limited to ephemeral tokens and non-sensitive features. Sensitive customer data is never serialized across nodes unless customer permits via config (for private deployments).
  - For private/self-hosted customers we provide a stronger option: in-place volume attachment or encrypted state handoff via customer-managed KMS.

- Routing and controller integration:
  - Smart router supports percentage-based canary routing and latency-based fallback to donor if recipient misses SLO.
  - Controller exposes APIs: start_handoff(tenant, mode, grace_window), status(lease_epoch), abort_handoff, finalize_handoff. These map to existing rollout primitives so product integrations (console, API) are straightforward.

- Autoscaling and burst economics:
  - Hot-standby nodes are part of a small reserved hot pool sized by heuristic (pool_size = min( max(1, floor(total_tenants * 0.02)), 8 )). They can be temporarily expanded by autoscaler if sustained demand is detected.
  - Billing: short burst usage during handoff is meterable as "burst seconds". Default policy bills burst usage to tenant; enterprise plans can absorb burst under negotiated contracts.

Isolation controls and guarantees:
- No cross-tenant execution: active handoff only runs models in same tenant namespace. Standby nodes must enforce ephemeral namespace boundaries and zero shared memory across tenants.
- Preemptive gating: if a recipient node detects a conflicting higher-priority tenant, it will gracefully roll back the handoff and route traffic back to donor.
- Audit trails: every transfer emits an immutable event log (who triggered, times, KV-delta size, checksum). This integrates with the Console for compliance reviews.

Operational runbook (quick playbook):
- Normal autoscaler triggered handoff: monitor handoff progress in Console -> if recipient latency > threshold for 3 consecutive 10s windows, abort and retry to alternate standby.
- Maintenance relocation: schedule soft handoff during low-traffic window, set grace_window=60s, disable billing for burst.
- Noisy neighbor emergency: operator can force-evict with short grace_window=5s but with increased tail-latency risk. Only SRE/admin roles allowed.

Metrics & observability:
- New metrics: handoff_count, handoff_duration_p50/p95, kv_delta_bytes, standby_warm_latency, post_handoff_error_rate, burst_seconds_consumed.
- Traces: distributed trace across donor->standby showing request path and applied prefix version.

UX/Console surface ideas:
- Handoff timeline view per-tenant (timeline slider showing percent traffic shift).
- Admin control to mark standby nodes for prewarming or drain.
- Billing preview showing estimated burst cost for recent handoffs.

Risks & mitigations:
- State inconsistency: dual-write window can create divergent ephemeral state. Mitigation: make dual-write idempotent using sequence numbers and reconcile pass at finalization.
- Privacy exposure: any state transfer increases attack surface. Mitigation: default compacted diffs + encryption + customer opt-in for deeper state transfer.
- Cost/overprovisioning: hot-standby pool may be underutilized. Mitigation: autoscaler reduces hot pool during quiet periods; opportunistic multi-tenant standby only when policy allows.

Open questions / decisions to make:
- Default billing policy for multi-tenant burst absorption (tenant pays vs pool pays).
- Exact format and size limits for KV diffs.
- Operator permission model for forced short grace handoffs.

Next steps / implementation plan (rough):
- Week 0–2: prototype controller APIs and a minimal smart-router percentage ramp feature (engineer: Owen).
- Week 3–6: runtime changes for dual-write idempotent mode and compacted KV diff format (engineer: Asha + infra).
- Week 7–9: implement standby prewarm orchestration + telemetry integration (owner: product-dedicated team).
- Week 10: dogfood in a small cohort of dedicated customers, collect latencies and KV delta sizes; iterate.

Appendix: short example sequence (operator-initiated):
  - admin: start_handoff(tenant-42, active, grace_window=30) -> controller picks standby node-n12
  - donor begins compacted-diff stream (10KB avg) to node-n12; node-n12 warms kernels and validates checksums
  - smart-router ramp: 0% -> 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100% (over 30s). Dual-write active until finalization
  - finalize: controller validates metrics, completes epoch handoff, donor drains and releases lease

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a draft meant to start architecture discussion with serving runtime and infra. Key asks: feasibility check for KV diff approach (serving-runtime), telemetry contract size (observability), cost model for billable burst seconds (finance/product). Please add notes inline or flag for the cross-team sync session next week.
